soft and easily broken, so it stays near its rock. It is found as pebbles in gulch gravel beside the bedrock ("pebbles of greenstone, serpentine, granitic rocks", Fry Gulch, Shenon 1933 USGS B846-B p.189) and as boulders and float below the bodies; the sheared kind falls apart ("Few pieces are larger than an inch in diameter", Ramp 1961 DOGAMI B52 p.62) and it rots away in old gravel ("The complete disintegration of the serpentine rocks in the Tertiary formation", Shenon 1933 p.183). In the lowest 11 miles of the Chetco River, below the biggest serpentine country in Oregon, ultramafic rocks with others "typically compose less than 10 percent of the sampled rock types" (USGS SIR 2010-5065 p.36). No source gives a wear rate for serpentine; the river step uses the rate of rock of the same hardness (limestone and marble, 2 percent a kilometre; Attal and Lave 2009), which is a convention.

a bar of a big Montana river: the stream access law lets the public use a river "without regard to the ownership of the land underlying the waters", on "its bed, and its banks up to the ordinary high-water mark" (MCA 23-2-301, 23-2-302), and the state's riverbeds are "held in trust for the people" (MCA 77-1-102). No rule read names picking up stones; the state's geological survey says "Most people find agates in the gravel bars along the active Yellowstone River channel" and that the law lets anyone walk the river "as long as they remain below the high-water mark" (MBMG 2023). Stay below the high-water mark, reach the river by a public access site, a bridge or a boat (the law gives no right "to enter onto or cross private property"), and do not collect inside a fishing access site.
